newsitem.title: UK: Bulgaria unrest may be silver lining for investors.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria unrest may be silver lining for investors.

text.p: Growing political unrest in Bulgaria may turn out to be good news for foreign investors who would prefer the ruling party of ex-communists out of power, replaced by a government more willing to reform a chaotic economy, analysts said on Monday.
"The situation in Bulgaria over the past year has been heading for disaster. Anything that raises the possiblity of change is a good thing," said Salomon Brothers analyst David Boren.
Protest demonstrations have mushroomed in the past two weeks and trade unions have launched strikes in support of opposition calls for a general election two years ahead of schedule.
Investors too have despaired of the ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party which has for two years presided over a deepening economic crisis, which analysts say have been marked by greed and incompetence.
"(The growing opposition) marginally improves the chances of there being a decent government," Merrill Lynch analyst Andrew Kenningham said.

But even if the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), seen as more foreign investor-friendly, were to win power it will still be a struggle to get its economy into shape and avoid a debt default.
"I think default is very likely in the next two years, but slightly less likely if the UDF is in power," Kenningham added.

Bulgaria has enough reserves to meet Brady bond debt repayments at the end of this month but may struggle to meet the next batch of payments in July unless it manages to win over the International Monetary Fund.
"I'm convinced the January payment is safe but there is significant doubt about the July payment," Boren said.
Bulgaria owes $135 million this month with its foreign reserves little more than $500 million.

The IMF insists Bulgaria introduce a currency board -- a system to prevent the government printing more money than it has to pay its bills -- before it will provide any loans and now says it will negotiate only when there is a stable government.
Prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned last month and efforts to appoint a new one have been stymied by outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev.
Bulgaria cannot expect any inflows of foreign finance until it has secured a deal with the IMF, analysts said.
ING Barings analyst Parvoleta Shtereva said Bulgarian debt prices were certain to remain volatile until the government was securely in place, but it was far from clear when that might be.

The protests have sent prices of Bulgarian Brady bonds -- which have the highest spreads over U.S. Treasuries in the emerging debt market -- lower on Monday only to prompt fresh buying by investors with a strong appetite for risk.
"But I think things are going to continue to look pretty nasty for a while. Prices could fall further," Salomon's Boren said.
